headline: High-risk write/conflict and cascading-error pathways exist; prompt-injection and leakage are lower but nonzero due to shared file/MCP surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: MinerU can use an MCP server and reads local document inputs; ms-swift can consume files and stdin/stdout. A shared file or MCP bridge could let attacker-controlled document text influence downstream instructions, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty about the exact orchestration escalates above low.
conditions: IF the orchestrator passes MinerU-extracted text into ms-swift prompts or stdin without sanitization, injection is plausible.
IF both agents share a workspace or MCP bridge, document content can cross trust boundaries.
mitigations: Disable automatic prompting from extracted text.
Insert a strict delimiter/schema wrapper around MinerU output.
Review any MCP route that forwards document text.
Use a separate workspace per agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-agent payloads.

B_data_leakage.rationale: MinerU touches PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, and OCR text; ms-swift reads files and handles hub/sdk tokens plus logs and checkpoints. If they share a workspace, sensitive document content can be copied into training outputs or logs. The pairwise leakage path is inferred rather than directly documented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory, document contents can be exposed through ms-swift logs or outputs.
IF MinerU extracts sensitive text and ms-swift ingests it for training or evaluation, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Use separate directories for inputs and outputs.
Redact secrets before handing text to ms-swift.
Turn off verbose logging.
Restrict file permissions on shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: MinerU has allowlisted network egress and MCP-based I/O, while ms-swift has shell, subprocess, install, read/write filesystem, and API access. Both can mutate files in overlapping workspaces, and ms-swift can create additional processes that race with MinerU. With no locking or shared-state guarantees, default concurrent use is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory, concurrent writes can clobber outputs.
IF ms-swift installs packages or spawns subprocesses while MinerU is running, state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories.
Run only one agent at a time on shared artifacts.
Disable package installation during shared runs.
Use file locks around mutable outputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: MinerU produces extracted text, tables, and OCR output that ms-swift can consume via files or stdin/stdout. ms-swift can then act through CLI/Python/API without an explicit verification step in the profiles. That makes A's extraction errors likely to cascade into B's downstream actions, and uncertainty about safeguards pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF MinerU output is used as authoritative input to ms-swift, extraction errors propagate.
IF ms-swift triggers training, evaluation, or API actions from that output, downstream mistakes become operational.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A output.
Add validation checks for extracted tables and OCR text.
Compare against source documents for critical fields.
Log provenance for every derived artifact.
requires-engineering: implement a verification gate between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: MinerU is documented as private/offline, while ms-swift explicitly handles hub tokens and can call external model APIs. If regulated document data from MinerU flows into ms-swift, residency and retention obligations may diverge. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated documents processed by MinerU are forwarded to ms-swift APIs, external retention policies apply.
IF the deployment requires offline-only handling, ms-swift's API use violates that requirement.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of ms-swift API calls.
Use local-only endpoints where possible.
Separate retention policies by data class.
Review token handling and logs.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
